#9686. Are Fintech Apps Putting Your Life Savings at Risk?

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

After 25 years in traditional banking, credit risk, and banking operations, I look at financial apps very differently than most tech professionals do. When a software engineer or a remote freelancer opens Wise, Revolut, PayPal, or Cash App, they see a masterpiece of modern user experience. You get a sleek dark-mode dashboard, instant multi-currency swaps, a heavy metal Visa or Mastercard debit card, and local account details or an IBAN where your employer or clients can wire your monthly paycheck. It looks like a bank, it moves money faster than the brick-and-mortar dinosaur down the street, and it does not charge you thirty dollars just to receive an international wire.

My eyes skip the interface entirely and go straight to the bottom of the screen. Down in the footer, usually printed in tiny eight-point gray font that nobody reads until their rent money disappears, sits the single most important sentence in your financial life. That sentence names the specific legal entity holding your balance and the regulatory license under which it operates.

In finance, user interface design means nothing when a company runs into trouble. A banking charter is not an aesthetic vibe. It is a specific, heavily supervised legal structure. When you use a nonbank fintech app as your primary checking account and store your salary or life savings inside it, you are often trading statutory deposit insurance and human accountability for a pretty screen. You are exposing your livelihood to pooled omnibus ledgers, hair-trigger compliance algorithms, and customer support queues run by chatbots.

This is no longer a fringe habit among digital nomads sitting in Bali coffee shops. According to the FDIC's National Survey of Unbanked and Underbanked Households, nearly half of all American households (49.7 percent) use nonbank online payment services like PayPal, Venmo, or Cash App. Even more striking, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's warning on nonbank payment apps notes that more than three-quarters of U.S. adults, and roughly 85 percent of young adults aged 18 to 29, use these platforms, with annual transaction volume projected to reach USD 1.6 trillion by 2027. Millions of smart people are leaving billions of dollars sitting inside apps that were never chartered to act as vaults.

An account number, a routing code, or a European IBAN only tells a payment rail where to deliver a message; it tells you nothing about how that money is legally protected once it lands. To understand the risk you are taking with your paycheck, you have to understand the structural divide between a licensed deposit-taking bank and an Electronic Money Institution (EMI) or money transmitter.

When you deposit money into a chartered commercial bank, your balance becomes a direct legal liability on that bank's balance sheet. Because licensed banks are allowed to lend out customer deposits and have direct access to central bank settlement accounts and liquidity facilities, governments force them into strict capital frameworks and mandatory, statutory deposit insurance schemes. In the United States, the FDIC's official deposit insurance rules guarantee deposits up to USD 250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Across the European Union, the European Union's Deposit Guarantee Schemes framework protects up to EUR 100,000 per person per bank. In the United Kingdom, the UK's Financial Services Compensation Scheme coverage rules automatically protect eligible bank deposits up to GBP 120,000 per person per banking license (following the limit increase from GBP 85,000 in December 2025).

Look at what happens when a real bank fails. If your chartered bank collapses on a Friday afternoon, statutory deposit insurance kicks in automatically. The FDIC typically makes insured funds available the very next business day, and the UK's FSCS pays out automatically within seven working days. Your rent check still clears.

Now compare that with an Electronic Money Institution or a state-licensed money transmitter. When you send USD 10,000 or EUR 10,000 to an EMI, you are not making a bank deposit. Legally, you are handing over real money in exchange for digital tokens of equivalent value called "e-money" or a stored-value balance. Because an EMI is forbidden from lending your money out like a bank, it does not participate in government deposit insurance. Instead, it protects your balance through a regulatory mechanism called "safeguarding."

Fintech marketing teams love to make safeguarding sound identical to deposit insurance, sometimes even arguing it is safer because your money is not being loaned out to mortgage borrowers. Having spent two and a half decades watching how financial plumbing behaves under stress, I can tell you that safeguarding and deposit insurance live on different planets when an institution goes bust.

Under safeguarding rules, the fintech takes your money and pools it together with the funds of millions of other users inside giant commingled accounts (known in banking as omnibus accounts) at partner commercial banks, or parks it in short-term government bonds and money market funds. For example, Wise's official safeguarding disclosure states plainly that Wise is not a bank and protects over GBP 18.1 billion in customer balances by holding a mix of short-term government bonds, money market funds, and cash in commercial banks.

Here is the catch nobody puts on the billboard. If an EMI goes bankrupt, there is no government agency standing by to wire your balance back to you next Tuesday. As the UK Financial Conduct Authority's guidance on non-bank payment service providers explicitly warns consumers, safeguarded funds are not protected by the FSCS. When an EMI fails, independent insolvency practitioners and liquidators take control of the company. They freeze the pooled omnibus accounts, audit the internal ledgers against the actual cash sitting at partner banks, and untangle who is owed what. Worse yet, as the FCA explicitly points out, you may not even get 100 percent of your money back, because the administrators and liquidators deduct their own hefty legal and administrative fees directly from the safeguarded customer pot before distributing whatever is left. That process does not take 48 hours. It takes months or even years.

What makes this even trickier for expats, remote workers, and frequent travelers is that a fintech's legal status changes depending on where you live when you sign up. You cannot judge an app by its global brand name.

Take Wise, Revolut, and PayPal, three platforms I see freelancers use every single day:

If you live in the United States or run a U.S. LLC for your freelance business, you have probably seen dozens of shiny neobank apps advertising "FDIC-insured up to USD 250,000 through our partner bank." That single marketing line has lulled millions of tech-savvy users into a false sense of security.

To see why, you need to understand how Banking-as-a-Service (BaaS) works under the hood. Obtaining a real U.S. banking charter takes years and tens of millions of dollars in regulatory capital. Most Silicon Valley fintech startups do not want to be banks. They want to build software. So they rent a charter from a small regional or community bank. Often, the startup does not even connect directly to that regional bank; instead, both sides plug into a BaaS "middleware" company that maintains the software ledger tracking customer transactions.

Your money sits in a giant pooled custodial account at the partner bank, usually titled "For the Benefit Of (FBO) Customers." For FDIC insurance to legally pass through that fintech app to you, the FDIC's pass-through deposit insurance regulations require three strict conditions to be met at all times: the funds must actually be owned by you (not the intermediary), the bank's own account records must explicitly disclose the custodial relationship, and accurate records maintained in the ordinary course of business must clearly identify every individual owner and their exact dollar balance.

What happens when the partner bank is perfectly healthy, solvent, and open for business, but the fintech app or the middleware company sitting in the middle goes bankrupt?

Thousands of everyday Americans found out the hard way when the BaaS middleware company Synapse collapsed. In FDIC Chairman Martin J. Gruenberg's statement on the Synapse bankruptcy, the regulator laid out the brutal anatomy of this failure. Consumers had placed their savings and paychecks into apps that prominently advertised FDIC insurance through partner banks like Evolve Bank & Trust. Most of those users had never even heard the name Synapse. Yet when Synapse filed for bankruptcy, tens of thousands of consumers had their life savings frozen for months because the customer funds were pooled into commingled custodial accounts and Synapse's internal ledgers did not match the balances recorded at the partner banks.

And where was the FDIC while families could not pay their mortgages or buy groceries? Sitting on the sidelines, legally unable to pay out a dime. As the FDIC's consumer warning on third-party banking apps states in black and white, nonbank companies themselves are never FDIC-insured, and FDIC deposit insurance only triggers when the chartered bank fails. If your fintech app or its middleware provider goes bankrupt and leaves behind a scrambled omnibus ledger, FDIC insurance does not bail you out. You are stuck waiting for bankruptcy judges and forensic accountants to argue over spreadsheets.

Even if your favorite fintech never comes close to insolvency, there is a much more common everyday hazard that hits independent professionals, remote workers, and expats every single week: the sudden, unannounced algorithmic account freeze.

Anyone who spends five minutes browsing forums for freelancers or digital nomads has seen the horror stories. Someone receives a legitimate USD 8,500 consulting payment from a new client, logs in from a hotel Wi-Fi network in Lisbon, or converts a chunk of euros into dollars, and suddenly their account is locked for a "routine security and compliance review."

From the outside, this looks like random cruelty. From the inside of banking operations, it is the predictable result of two structural forces: partner-bank paranoia and hyper-scaler unit economics.

Traditional banks freeze cards and flag wires too. I worked inside regulated banks for 25 years, and I have seen plenty of clumsy bank compliance departments hold up legitimate transfers. The difference is what happens five minutes after the freeze occurs.

When a traditional brick-and-mortar bank locks your account on the 28th of the month while your rent is due, you have a physical escalation path. You can put your passport, your tax return, and your signed client contract into a folder, walk through the glass doors of a local branch, and sit down across the desk from a branch manager. A branch manager cannot wave a magic wand to override a federal AML hold, and anyone who tells you otherwise does not understand banking law. What a branch manager can do is verify your physical identity on the spot, scan your certified documents directly into the internal compliance portal, and pick up an internal phone extension to speak with a human investigator in the back office. You have a pulse, a face, and a physical presence in their lobby.

Now try doing that with an app-only fintech. There is no branch. Most of the time, there isn't even a working customer service phone line that connects to a human being. Look at Revolut's European banking terms or its U.S. agreement: the listed phone number is an automated line strictly for freezing a lost card, explicitly stating it cannot connect you to a human agent.

Your entire relationship with the institution exists inside a smartphone app, and your only real communication channel is the in-app support chat. Here is the Kafkaesque trap that catches thousands of users off guard: when the compliance algorithm suspends or restricts your account login, you often cannot even open the app to reach the in-app chat. You are locked out of the building, and the help desk is inside the building. You are left sending desperate emails into a generic support inbox, getting copy-pasted AI chatbot replies telling you that "our specialized team is reviewing your case and cannot provide a timeline," while your salary, your tax money, and your grocery budget sit frozen in digital purgatory for 30, 60, or 90 days.

Let me be crystal clear: I am not telling you to delete Wise, Revolut, or PayPal. I use fintech apps myself almost every week. They are brilliant at what they were originally built to do, which is slashing foreign exchange markups, splitting dinner bills, and moving money across borders without letting old-school banks rob you on wire fees.

The mistake is confusing a great payment rail with a safe vault. If you want all the speed and convenience of modern fintech without ever waking up to find your rent money held hostage by an algorithm or a bankruptcy court, follow these four rules.

Think about how you use a physical leather wallet when you walk out your front door. You put USD 100 or EUR 150 in cash and a couple of cards in your pocket because it is convenient for buying coffee, paying for a taxi, or picking up groceries. You would never stuff your entire monthly salary and USD 40,000 of life savings into your back pocket and walk around town.

Apply that exact same logic to every fintech app on your phone. Use Wise, Revolut, Venmo, or Cash App as transit corridors and spending wallets. Before you leave a balance sitting in an app overnight, ask yourself one ruthless question: If an algorithm froze this exact dollar amount tomorrow morning for 60 days, would I miss rent, default on a bill, or be unable to buy plane tickets home? If the answer is yes, you have too much money on the app. Top it up when you need to spend or convert currencies, and keep the balance lean.

Your financial foundation should be boring. Your primary paycheck and your six-month emergency living reserve belong in a dull, heavily regulated, directly insured brick-and-mortar bank with physical branches in the country where you legally reside.

I do not care if that traditional bank has an ugly mobile app from 2016 or pays zero percent interest on its checking account. You are not hiring your primary bank for entertainment. You are hiring it for statutory deposit insurance (FDIC, DGS, or FSCS), direct central-bank settlement access, and a physical door you can walk through if your phone is stolen or your account is flagged. If an international client insists on paying you via Wise or PayPal because it is easier for their accounting department, let the payment hit the app and immediately transfer the settled funds out to your boring local bank account.

In banking operations, we never build a system with a single point of failure. Neither should you. Even the best chartered bank can suffer an IT outage or flag your card while you are traveling abroad.

Always maintain active, funded accounts at two completely independent financial institutions running on two separate card networks. For example, keep your primary salary and savings at a major traditional bank with a Visa debit or credit card, and keep a secondary buffer of one month's living expenses at a second, unrelated bank (plus a modest travel spending balance on a Mastercard-backed fintech app). And check the fine print to make sure your two banks do not share the same underlying banking charter or BaaS sponsor bank. True redundancy means that if Institution A locks your account on a Friday night at an airport hotel checkout in Tokyo, you can calmly pull out Card B from a completely separate banking group, pay your bill, and deal with the paperwork on Monday.

If you are a freelancer, creator, or online merchant collecting revenue through PayPal, Stripe, Payoneer, or Venmo, stop treating your processor dashboard like a business savings account. Payment processors and merchant aggregators have the most aggressive automated reserve and hold policies in the financial industry because they are on the hook for chargebacks and buyer disputes.

Understand the difference between settlement timing and payout schedules. For instance, Stripe's documentation on payout schedules and settlement speeds explains that setting your account to "daily payouts" only controls how often available funds are pushed to your bank, not how many working days it takes for a pending customer payment to settle. Once your incoming revenue has genuinely settled and cleared any required refund buffer, sweep it out to your chartered business bank account on a regular, predictable schedule. Keep clean PDF copies of your client contracts, invoices, and monthly statements stored offline on your computer, and avoid bouncing money back and forth between multiple personal wallets, which looks like textbook money-laundering "layering" to automated bank filters.

Financial technology has given everyday people and independent workers tools that only multinational corporate treasuries had twenty years ago. We should use those tools for everything they are worth.

Just remember who is sitting on the other side of the glass screen. A shiny metal card and a friendly push notification do not rewrite banking law, and a partner-bank logo at the bottom of a landing page does not turn a software startup into a fortress. Let fintech apps handle the movement of your money, let a real chartered bank guard the storage of your wealth, and never give a single algorithm the power to lock you out of your life.

The Cashless Scam: How Visa and Mastercard Tax Every Bite You Eat

#9682. Telegram Bots and Mini Apps on Localhost: setWebhook, the Secret-Token Header, and the New Origin Check

Posted on Nov 17 • Originally published at instatunnel.my • Fully Autonomous

Telegram can only deliver updates to a public HTTPS address, and localhost is not one. Since July 20, 2026, Mini Apps have a second constraint. Telegram now blocks Mini App methods when they are called from a different origin than the Mini App’s own domain. Together, these two facts make your tunnel URL a first-class piece of configuration, not a throwaway detail.

This guide covers developing a Telegram bot and Mini App against a local machine:

Telegram released Bot API 10.2 on July 14, 2026. According to the official changelog, that release also hardened Mini App security by disallowing Mini App methods from origins different from the original Mini App domain. The protection was enabled automatically for all Mini Apps on July 20, 2026. Bots can opt out through the BotFather Mini App. Opting out means taking responsibility for ensuring the Mini App has no links to untrusted sites. Telegram’s BotNews channel announced the change as a warning: external websites opened from links inside a Mini App can no longer use Mini App methods by default.

Other 10.2 additions are worth knowing about, because they show up in your webhook payloads:

None of the 10.2–10.4 announcements change how setWebhook or the secret-token header work. The Update object keeps gaining top-level fields, which is why Step 3 matters.

A webhook is an outgoing HTTPS POST from Telegram’s servers to your URL. Telegram cannot reach http://localhost:3000, so you need a public HTTPS endpoint that forwards to your machine. Telegram’s documented requirements:

A tunnel satisfies all of this at once. It gives you a public hostname with a valid certificate on port 443 and forwards traffic to a local port such as 3000.

There is one exception for the bot side only. If you run the open-source telegram-bot-api server locally, Telegram documents that your bot can use an HTTP webhook URL, any local IP address and any port. That removes the tunnel for webhook delivery. It does not make a Mini App reachable from a phone, because the Telegram client still has to load the Mini App URL.

Each bot has exactly one webhook URL. Calling setWebhook again replaces it. Use a separate development bot, created through BotFather, so your experiments never redirect production traffic.

Start your local server, start your tunnel, then register the public URL:

An allowed_updates change does not apply to updates that were created before the call, so a few unwanted updates can still arrive.

To return to polling, call deleteWebhook.

If you pass secret_token to setWebhook, Telegram includes it in every webhook request in the X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token header. The token must be 1 to 256 characters, using only A-Z, a-z, 0-9, _ and -.

This matters because your tunnel URL is public. Without a secret, anyone who discovers the URL can POST forged updates, and nothing in the request identifies Telegram. If you set no token, Telegram sends no header at all.

The mechanism is a shared secret, not a signature. Nothing is computed over the body, so a leaked secret lets an attacker forge requests until you rotate it. Rotation is simple: call setWebhook again with a new value. Hookdeck’s guide also lists Telegram’s published source ranges (149.154.160.0/20 and 91.108.4.0/22) as an optional second layer, and notes that they may change.

Telegram does not publish a response timeout, so don’t let delivery depend on slow work. Persist or queue the update first, return 200, then process. If you return 200 and then crash, the update is gone, so store it before you acknowledge.

Telegram treats any response other than a 2xx as a failed delivery. It repeats the request and gives up after what it calls a “reasonable amount of attempts”, without publishing a schedule. That has a sharp consequence for strict parsers. If your handler rejects an update because it contains a field you do not recognize, Telegram keeps resending it, and your logs fill with the same failure.

An Update contains update_id plus at most one other field, and the set of those fields keeps growing: managed_bot, guest_message, subscription, stopped_message_generation and, in 10.4, widget queries. A decoder that fails on unexpected keys can start returning errors even though nothing is wrong with your bot. Practical rules:

Use allowed_updates as a second layer. Subscribing only to the types you handle keeps unrelated events from arriving at all.

A Mini App is a web page that runs inside Telegram’s in-app browser and talks to the client through window.Telegram.WebApp. In development you point it at your tunnel URL:

Keep the hostname identical everywhere it appears. The origin check below makes that more than tidiness.

Production Mini Apps are served over HTTPS, which any tunnel provides. Telegram’s separate test environment is the exception. It uses its own account and its own bot, and its docs allow plain HTTP Mini App links there. You call it through https://api.telegram.org/bot/test/METHOD_NAME.

Two framework gotchas come up repeatedly:

To debug inside the Telegram client, Telegram documents these options:

When the Mini App opens, window.Telegram.WebApp.initData contains a signed query string. It is empty if the Mini App was launched from a keyboard button or from inline mode. Never trust initDataUnsafe or any user object on the client. Send the raw string to your backend and verify it with Telegram’s documented algorithm:

Telegram only says to check auth_date to avoid outdated data. The one-hour window is your choice. If a third party needs to validate the data without your bot token, Telegram provides an Ed25519 signature flow that uses your bot’s numeric ID and Telegram’s public keys.

Before July 20, 2026, any page opened inside your Mini App’s webview could call Telegram.WebApp.* methods such as close(), expand(), the main button or sendData(). Now those calls are allowed only from the Mini App’s own domain. Telegram’s changelog calls it the “original Mini App domain”. Third-party documentation describes it as the domain registered in BotFather.

What this means in practice, per Leadgram’s write-up of the change:

The rule is about hostnames. These consequences follow from it:

A debugging checklist for when a Mini App method suddenly stops working in development:

If a foreign page only calls close() or openLink(), Leadgram’s suggested fix is replacing the call with an ordinary https://t.me/... link or a redirect.

The BotFather Mini App lets you disable the protection, but Telegram’s wording is a warning: by doing so you take responsibility for ensuring the Mini App links to no untrusted sites. Opting out restores the old behavior, where any page inside the webview can drive the app, which is exactly the hole Telegram closed. Opting out to make a development setup work is the wrong fix when the real problem is an origin mismatch. Fix the mismatch, keep the protection on, and reserve opt-out for cases where you fully control every page the Mini App can navigate to.

Every piece of Telegram configuration in this article is keyed to a URL: the webhook endpoint, the Mini App domain, and the origin Telegram compares against when a page calls a Mini App method. When the URL changes on every restart, you re-register all three each time. One forgotten update produces confusing symptoms, such as silent webhooks or Mini App methods that worked yesterday failing today.

What the documented free options give you:

Mind the ngrok interstitial. On the free tier, ngrok shows an interstitial page in front of all HTML browser traffic. ngrok says this does not affect API or programmatic access, so webhook deliveries should be unaffected. A Mini App page loaded in Telegram’s webview is HTML browser traffic, so users may see the warning page. ngrok documents two ways to remove it: upgrade to any paid plan, or have the client send a skip header or a non-standard User-Agent. The header route is awkward for a page that Telegram’s webview loads.

Other tunneling services offer stable subdomains on free or paid tiers. Check your provider’s current terms for subdomain persistence, session length and browser-warning pages before you depend on them.

Which ports can Telegram send webhooks to? 443, 80, 88 and 8443. A tunnel exposes port 443 and forwards to whatever local port you use.

What happens if my webhook returns an error? Telegram treats non-2xx responses as failures and retries, giving up after “a reasonable amount of attempts”. An endpoint that errors on unexpected input can cause repeated deliveries.

Can I skip the tunnel and use getUpdates? For bot logic, yes, as long as no webhook is set. A Mini App still needs a URL the Telegram client can load, so it needs a public HTTPS hostname. The exceptions are the test environment and a local Bot API server, which only covers the bot side.

Is the secret token mandatory? No, but without it nothing in a request identifies Telegram, and anyone who finds your tunnel URL can send forged updates.

Is Bot API 10.2 the latest version? No. Bot API 10.3 (August 24, 2026) and 10.4 (November 9, 2026) have been released since. The webhook and Mini App origin behavior described here still applies.

#9680. Dreamteam Raises $53M Led by Accel to Rebuild the $100B CRM Market Around AI Teammates

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

Every sales team runs on a story about its customers. Who is the real decision-maker, what made the buyer pause on price, which rival came up on the last call and what the team promised to send by Friday. For 25 years, the software meant to hold that story has asked salespeople to type it in by hand. Most of the time, they don't.

That gap sits inside one of the largest markets in business software. Salesforce earned $21.6 billion of CRM revenue in 2024, a 20.7% share that implies a global customer relationship management (CRM) market of about $104 billion (our arithmetic), while the category grew 12.8% in a single year. Yet salespeople still spend only 40% of their time selling, losing the rest to research, admin and data entry that their systems were supposed to remove.

Dreamteam is built on a different design, one where the CRM listens and acts without waiting to be told. The AI-native CRM, founded in 2025 by three former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million across its Seed and Series A rounds in a round led by Accel, with participation from Premji Invest and from Together Fund, the company's first institutional investor and seed lead. Hundreds of companies already use it, including teams at Plex, invideo and Lookout.ai.

Salesforce has led CRM revenue for 12 straight years, with Microsoft its nearest rival at $5.45 billion, while Adobe, Oracle, SAP and HubSpot divide much of what remains. The market is far from saturated. It grew 12.8% in 2024, faster than Salesforce's own 9.5%, which nudged the leader's share down from 21.7% to 20.7% as spending spread across more vendors.

What has barely changed is the design. Legacy CRMs were built around structured fields and hand-coded workflows, which record a deal stage or a contract value well. They struggle with the signals that actually decide deals, such as a prospect who sounds unsure, a board that has started questioning costs or a competitor named in passing on a call. Every new tool a company adds to fill that gap scatters the customer story across one more system.

Salesforce's 2026 State of Sales survey of 4,050 sales professionals found that sellers spend 40% of their time selling. The other 60% goes to research, data entry, admin and internal work. Nearly half of sellers say they lack the bandwidth for proper outreach, even though prospecting already eats close to a full workday each week.

Sales teams have already chosen their fix. 87% of sales organizations use AI in some form, while sellers expect prospect research time to fall 34% and email drafting time to fall 36% once AI is fully in place. The obstacle is data. 51% of sales leaders using AI say disconnected systems are slowing their projects, which is exactly the gap an AI-native CRM is designed to close.

AI agents, software that can carry out tasks on a person's behalf, are moving from pilots into daily sales work. 54% of sellers have already used one, 55% use AI for prospecting and nearly nine in ten plan to use agents by 2027. The best teams are moving first, as top performers are 1.7 times more likely than underperformers to use prospecting agents.

An agent is only as good as what it can see. 79% of high performers prioritize data hygiene, compared with 54% of underperformers, while 74% of sales professionals say they are focused on cleaning their data. A CRM that captures context automatically hands every agent a complete, current view of each customer without that clean-up work.

Dreamteam's $53 million spans its Seed and Series A rounds. Accel led the funding, while Premji Invest and Together Fund participated. Together Fund, founded by Freshworks co-founder Girish Mathrubootham, led the seed round and was Dreamteam's first institutional investor, which means the founders' former colleague backed them from the first day.

The raise puts Dreamteam among the best-funded AI-native CRM startups so far. Attio raised a $52 million Series B in August 2025 led by GV, while Day AI raised a $20 million Series A in February 2026 led by Sequoia, so Dreamteam's total is about 2.7 times Day AI's round (our arithmetic). The pattern is clear: investors are funding a new generation of CRMs designed for AI from the first line of code, not legacy systems with AI added on top.

Dreamteam starts by listening. It connects to a team's email, calendar, meetings and other tools, then builds what it calls the Company Brain, a living memory of the business. From every interaction it pulls out the signals that matter, including buyer intent, objections and price hesitation, competitor mentions, stakeholder dynamics and the commitments each side made. The CRM updates itself, so salespeople no longer have to.

Four specialized AI teammates then put that memory to work. Rachel, the research assistant, enriches every account and contact. Sally, the sales assistant, prepares for meetings, drafts follow-up emails and manages tasks. Raj, the RevOps partner, watches the pipeline, flags deals at risk and sharpens forecasts, while Alex, the CRM administrator, sets up and runs the system in plain language.

People stay in charge of the result. Sales teams review and approve the actions their AI teammates propose, while sales leaders can ask questions that legacy CRMs struggle to answer, such as which deals are stalling and why. Each teammate arrives trained for its job, so companies do not have to build and train their own agents before they see value.

Dreamteam is also built to work with other AI. It offers a first-class API and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, the open standard that lets AI assistants connect to outside software, so teams can work with their CRM from tools such as Claude. Its Magic Apps feature brings vibe coding, building software by describing it in plain language, into the CRM, letting business users create custom apps and dashboards without writing code.

Dreamteam built its product alongside a small group of fast-growing, AI-forward sales teams, which kept it anchored in real sales workflows from day one. Today hundreds of companies use it across AI, online media, healthcare, manufacturing and consulting.

At invideo, the enterprise sales team began with a small pilot and soon rolled Dreamteam out to the whole team, with the CRM reviewing customer interactions each morning and surfacing insights the team had never been able to see. Plex co-founder Scott Olechowski has said the product hits the sweet spot between simplicity and powerful AI, singling out how well it works with existing AI tools such as Claude, while DMS Health chief executive Patrick Doyle believes it is far ahead of what other CRMs offer.

Dreamteam was founded by Anand Venkatraman, Ramesh Parthasarathy and Senthil Kanthaswamy, former senior executives at Freshworks who helped scale that company from its early startup days through its IPO. Each brings more than 25 years of experience building and selling B2B software. Between them, they have spent time at Microsoft, Salesforce, Akamai and Sun Microsystems.

They have also been building with AI longer than most. The founders shipped AI applications in the GPT-2 era and scaled them to tens of thousands of businesses, then watched traditional CRMs leave teams with stale pipelines and unreliable forecasts. When AI models learned to reason over context, they concluded the CRM could finally be rebuilt from the ground up. Dreamteam is headquartered in Sacramento, California.

Dreamteam's ambitions reach past the sales team. The company is building a shared intelligence layer across the full customer lifecycle, from the first conversation through customer success to upsells, while Magic Apps lets each business shape the CRM around how it actually works.

Every generation of CRM has been defined by a platform shift. Siebel rode on-premise software, Salesforce rode the cloud and Freshworks proved a new challenger could scale to IPO. AI is the next shift, while the market Dreamteam is chasing is worth more than $100 billion. With $53 million, hundreds of customers and founders who have already built one enterprise software company to IPO, Dreamteam is positioned to show what a CRM looks like when it does the work itself.

#9679. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9677. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

For more fall baking inspiration, check out our Fall Flavor Edit.

#9676. Google ADK vs Strands: guía técnica y despliegue en AWS

Hace poco hice el curso de Agentes de la Academia GEAR de Google, donde experimenté con sesiones, state, tools, modelos locales y ejecución de código. En este artículo comparo Google ADK con Strands Agents a partir de un mismo caso real, un pipeline multiagente que construye un knowledge graph. También muestro cómo desplegarlo en Amazon Bedrock AgentCore con Terraform, cómo invocarlo y los resultados.

Google ADK y Strands Agents (cuyo SDK hoy la documentación llama Strands Harness SDK) son dos frameworks open source para construir agentes de IA en Python, y los dos corren en AWS. La diferencia está en cómo piensan el problema: ADK pone primero la estructura (un grafo de nodos y aristas que se define en código) y trae un entorno de desarrollo visual, mientras que Strands parte de un agente que decide con el modelo y suma patrones (Graph, Swarm, Workflow) cuando hace falta estructura.

En este artículo comparo los dos con un caso real, el mismo pipeline multiagente que construí con Strands en una serie anterior, reescrito con ADK 2.12.0 y Amazon Nova vía Bedrock, y desplegado en AgentCore.

ADK (Agent Development Kit) es el framework open source de Google para construir, evaluar y desplegar agentes. Tiene SDKs en Python, TypeScript, Go, Java y Kotlin, está optimizado para Gemini y admite otros modelos mediante integraciones como LiteLLM, Ollama o vLLM.

Un agente mínimo se crea en una carpeta con un agent.py que define root_agent, el único elemento obligatorio. Las tools son funciones Python con type hints y docstring. ADK las envuelve solo en un FunctionTool, y en ADK Python no existe el decorador @tool.

Para programar y ejecutar un ejemplo funcional en Python hacen falta tres cosas:

Según lo que se use, hay extras que se instalan aparte:

El comando adk create mi_agente crea una estructura mínima. Pregunta qué modelo se va a usar y guarda la configuración en el .env:

Con GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=TRUE, ADK ignora la API key y pide credenciales de Vertex AI. Para probar, ejecutar desde la carpeta padre adk run mi_agente (consola) o adk web (navegador). Ambos cargan el .env solos; si en cambio se corre un script propio, hay que llamar a load_dotenv() antes de importar el agente.

Para usar un modelo que no es Gemini, como Amazon Nova en Bedrock, solo se cambia el model por un LiteLlm (requiere el extra [extensions]). Las credenciales salen de la cadena estándar de AWS. Si el agente corre en tu máquina, usa el perfil configurado en la AWS CLI. Si está desplegado en AWS, usa el rol IAM que tiene asignado.

Las piezas que más se usan al pasar del prototipo a algo real:

Estos tres detalles los descubrí realizando pequeñas pruebas:

En ADK, el servicio de sesiones y el Runner son asíncronos. Mi primer script de prueba en el curso lo escribí con hábitos síncronos y no funcionaba por dos motivos:

En Strands con Python, invocar un agente es una llamada síncrona (agent("...")) y el session manager que se le pasa al crearlo guarda la conversación y el state por su cuenta. En ADK el control es explícito: se crea la sesión, se ejecuta y se vuelve a leer.

El state de una sesión es un diccionario que comparten agentes, tools y nodos. El prefijo de la clave define su alcance:

Con InMemorySessionService, todo esto vive en la memoria del proceso. Para que user: y app: sobrevivan a un reinicio hace falta un servicio persistente, como DatabaseSessionService.

adk web es una interfaz de desarrollo local, se levanta una app estilo chat en el navegador que muestra, para cada mensaje, el grafo del workflow, el state de la sesión, los eventos y las trazas con tokens y tiempos. En la documentación de Strands no hay un equivalente. Más abajo muestro cómo se visualiza con el caso práctico.

ADK 2.x ofrece varias formas de coordinar agentes (workflows):

Las clases de plantilla SequentialAgent, ParallelAgent y LoopAgent todavía funcionan, pero en el código de ADK 2.12 están marcadas como deprecated. Si se arranca un proyecto nuevo, usar Workflow.

Strands ordena lo mismo en patrones: Agents as tools, Graph, Swarm y Workflow, más un wrapper para implementar A2A que permite usar un agente remoto igual que uno local. Lo que los distingue de acuerdo a mis prácticas, es cómo se determina el camino de ejecución: en Graph se definen nodos y aristas con condiciones opcionales, en Swarm los agentes se pasan el control por su cuenta de manera autonoma, y Workflow es un grafo de tareas con dependencias.

Para comparar los dos frameworks conviene ordenar sus mecanismos con una sola pregunta: ¿quién decide el siguiente paso? En un extremo lo decide el código escrito por el desarrollador; en el otro, el modelo en tiempo de ejecución.

Posición orientativa según la documentación oficial de cada framework.

Para comparar con algo concreto, reescribí en ADK el pipeline de mi artículo sobre Graph en Strands: el ejemplo toma el abstract de un paper y lo convierte en un knowledge graph, una lista de entidades y relaciones sujeto → predicado → objeto. Sirve para resumir quién hizo qué en un texto, conectar conocimiento entre documentos o alimentar una base de grafos. 📦 El código Python original en Strands está en strands-graph.

📦 El repositorio de la versión ADK está en adk-knowledge-graph. Todo el detalle (instalación, pruebas, evals, despliegue con Terraform, costos y limpieza) está en el README del repositorio.

La topología es la misma en los dos frameworks: tres extractores en paralelo, un agregador que une sus resultados y un validador que puede devolver el borrador para revisión.

Cada agente LLM tiene su color; los nodos de código (funciones y JoinNode) tienen borde punteado.

En ADK, el grafo completo se declara en un solo lugar:

En Strands con TypeScript el default de Graph es AND, así que el problema del join es propio del SDK de Python.

El repositorio tiene dos versiones del multiagente: la del pipeline fijo de tres extractores (kg_pipeline), que es la que se compara con Strands, y una versión ampliada para textos largos (kg_pipeline_docs), que divide el documento en fragmentos, lanza un extractor por fragmento y va acumulando el grafo entre mensajes. La versión ampliada es la que después despliego en AWS.

En la versión ampliada para textos largos (kg_pipeline_docs)

adk web levanta una interfaz en el navegador (por defecto en http://localhost:8000) para conversar con los agentes y ver qué hacen por dentro (interfaz web). Se ejecuta desde el directorio padre de la carpeta del agente.

Con un Workflow, la interfaz dibuja el grafo y resalta el nodo del evento seleccionado en el panel de eventos. Además muestra el state de la sesión y una vista de trazas con cada llamada al modelo, sus tokens y su duración.

En la traza se ve el paralelismo: los tres extractores corren al mismo tiempo, unos 2 segundos cada uno, y la ejecución completa tarda 5 segundos. En la primera ejecución de cada proceso no es así: un extractor arranca y los otros dos esperan unos 7 segundos, mientras se inicializa el cliente de Bedrock (LiteLLM, boto3, credenciales y conexión TLS).

ADK Web es solo para desarrollo, por eso escucha en 127.0.0.1 por defecto. Para producción se usa adk api_server o un servicio propio. En la documentación de Strands no hay una interfaz local equivalente: la observabilidad se resuelve con trazas OpenTelemetry que se exportan a la herramienta que se prefiera. Es la diferencia de experiencia de desarrollo más grande entre los dos frameworks.

Los dos frameworks evalúan con el mismo esquema: casos de prueba, el agente que se ejecuta y un evaluador que puntúa el resultado. Cambia dónde vive cada parte:

En todo lo que muestra la tabla "Qué resuelve ADK de otra manera": el join sin código extra, la lógica determinista dentro del grafo, los loops con salida en código y adk web para depurar.

ADK es una librería, no un servicio de Google. La documentación oficial indica que el agente se puede empaquetar y ejecutar en cualquier entorno que admita contenedores. En AWS hay tres destinos naturales:

Para el knowledge graph elegí AgentCore Runtime, y desplegué la versión ampliada para textos largos (kg_pipeline_docs), porque es la que acumula el grafo entre mensajes. Pensé en cómo se usaría el agente: un investigador abre un proyecto, pega secciones de un paper y ve crecer el grafo. Son pocos usuarios, cada pedido tarda entre 5 y 20 segundos y el grafo tiene que durar mientras trabaja. Un contenedor encendido todo el día no se justifica, y AgentCore resuelve las sesiones por su cuenta.

Una aclaración sobre la comparación con Strands: mi versión en Strands (strands-graph) la construí para aprender orquestación y la probé solo en local, así que no la desplegué en AgentCore. Lo que se afirma sobre el despliegue de Strands se apoya en su documentación oficial, no en una prueba propia.

AgentCore ejecuta cada runtimeSessionId en su propia microVM y mantiene el contexto entre invocaciones. Si ese id se usa como session_id de ADK, el InMemorySessionService vive en la memoria de esa microVM y el grafo incremental crece entre llamadas, sin base de datos.

Rol IAM acotado para todo el recorrido: leer el zip, invocar solo Nova 2 Lite y escribir logs.

El adaptador sigue el ejemplo oficial de AWS para ADK (Use any agent framework). Lo único propio es usar el id de sesión de AgentCore:

AgentCore admite dos formas de desplegar: una imagen de contenedor en ECR o un zip con el código en S3 (despliegue directo de código). Elegí el zip porque no hace falta Docker y el paquete entra holgado en el límite de 250 MB: pesa unos 72 MB.

El recurso del runtime es el centro de la configuración:

Dos detalles de esa configuración. El provider de AWS debe ser ~> 6.22: el recurso existe desde la 6.17, pero code_configuration (el despliegue con zip) llegó en la 6.22, y con una versión anterior el código no compila. Y network_mode = "PUBLIC" es lo que usé en la prueba; no probé el modo VPC, que sería lo que habría que evaluar antes de llevar algo así a producción.

La seguridad del rol vale una mirada más detallada, porque es lo que el plan permite revisar. Dos extractos de main.tf:

Para ser más específica en cuanto a lo "acotado" del rol, este lee un único objeto de S3 y solo invoca ese modelo, pero X-Ray usa resources = ["*"] y PutMetricData va con * limitado por el namespace bedrock-agentcore. Son comodines que la documentación de AgentCore permite en esos servicios, pero no son un mínimo privilegio absoluto. Y quien invoca el runtime también necesita permisos IAM propios: el script de invocación del repositorio invoke.py usa boto3, así que las credenciales del usuario deben permitir bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime.

Las dependencias se instalan para Linux arm64 aunque el zip se arme en Windows o macOS, con pip install --platform manylinux2014_aarch64 --only-binary=:all:. Pero pip genera los scripts de consola para la máquina donde corre: en Windows, archivos .exe que no sirven en AgentCore. El script de empaquetado los regenera como lanzadores de Linux.

El log group del runtime queda con retención indefinida. Lo crea AgentCore con el id del runtime en el nombre, así que Terraform no puede crearlo antes, y la retención a nivel cuenta exige un mínimo de 30 días. La solución fue un terraform_data que, creado el runtime, fija la retención en 1 día con la AWS CLI y borra el log group en terraform destroy.

ADK ya genera trazas de OpenTelemetry (spans) por cada nodo, agente y llamada al modelo: las mismas que muestra adk web. Para verlas en la consola de AgentCore no hace falta escribir código de trazas, alcanzó con dos pasos:

Los nodos del workflow aparecen con los mismos nombres que en el código, con el modelo y los tokens de cada llamada.

En la prueba con la versión ampliada, tres textos del mismo paper llevaron el grafo de 9 a 40 y a 74 relaciones, y la tercera invocación, hecha en un comando aparte, conservó las 40 anteriores. La limitación: AgentCore cierra la microVM tras 15 minutos sin actividad (o 1 hora de vida, según la configuración), y una invocación posterior con el mismo id empieza con el grafo vacío. Para conservarlo hay que guardarlo fuera de la sesión, por ejemplo en S3 o con AgentCore Memory. El costo de la prueba fue mínimo: unos USD 0,01 en tokens por texto largo y menos de USD 0,01 por sesión de AgentCore.

⭐ La lección se repite después de construir el mismo pipeline con ADK y Strands: el framework importa menos que el harness determinista que rodea a los agentes. En este caso de uso, ese harness son los nodos de código que dividen la entrada, validan la salida, deciden las rutas y cortan los bucles. El modelo propone, pero es el harness el que decide qué se acepta.

#9675. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

In this article, we have taken a look at some of the biggest benefits associated with using sellfy for eCommerce. Once you compare these benefits to what you get with other platforms such as Shopify, you should find that it is worth your time to consider sellfy for your business. #9672. An embedded form or survey builder still ships skip logic and scoring in the browser

Form and survey builders often embed a runtime in the customer’s page: a script tag, a webpack chunk, or a Web Component. The pitch is instant skip logic, live validation, calculated scores, and no round-trip between questions. That runtime is JavaScript, and it usually includes the definition of the form itself.

If the value of your product is the engine — branching, scoring, price quotes, qualification — then that engine is in the browser. This article is about what an embedded form runtime actually exposes, what must be re-checked on the server, and how to protect the engine you still have to ship.

Minifying the runtime will rename pickNext. It will not hide "disqualify", a distinctive weight, or a question you thought was secret because the UI had not reached it yet.

This is the part teams regret after a launch. A hiring screen, a pricing quiz, a medical-style symptom tree, or a lead-qualification form sometimes puts the "real" criteria in client-side skip logic: reject if salary is below a number, skip the expensive plan if the company size is small, show a deluxe upsell only when the score is high.

Assume anyone can read those criteria. If they must stay unpublished — interview answer keys, fraud signals, medical cutoffs, unpublished prices — do not put them in the embed. Fetch the next question from the server, or at least re-evaluate the result on the server before it means anything.

Submitted answers should also go to your server in raw form. A client-computed score: 97 is a suggestion.

A snappy runtime is still the right UX for most marketing forms. Validation, animations, save-and-resume, and non-sensitive branching can stay in the browser. For the proprietary engine:

A JS VM obfuscator compiles that function to a custom bytecode and ships a small interpreter. Pretty-printing the chunk no longer reconstructs the original scoring routine; you get bytecode and a dispatcher. That is slower than a thin JSON walker, which is why you protect the engine, not the entire form UI.

VEILVM is a browser-based JSVMP workspace you can point at one extracted function before you wire protection into CI. Protection raises the cost of casual inspection and wholesale reuse. It does not make a public form definition a secret, and it does not replace a server-side score.

If you want to try VM protection on a single extracted function, VEILVM runs in the browser with no sign-up: 3 free runs a day, up to 5 KB per file (resets at 00:00 UTC). A free account raises the input limit to 30 KB. Pro is $9/month or $79/year and adds an API so the protection step can run in CI. Standard requests are processed in memory and are not written to logs. Start at https://vm.ldvmp.com.

#9670. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

Find our high-extraction Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour online.

#9668. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing.

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

Sounds like you're biased for Grammarly. Not really that informative if you're already leaning towards one to begin with. Still, it was an interesting read. Tell me, do you use Grammarly with your day-to-day writing/blogging?

I use the paid versions of both Grammarly and Pro Writing Aid. Both of them have issues:- Grammarly IS more focused on nonfiction than fiction. If you're writing fiction, you may find Grammarly's insistence on "Conciseness" annoying. They seem to want to take the soul out of your writing, which is fine for a corporate report or technical manual, but not for your Great American Novel.- Grammarly pushes features on users that are not ready for prime time. It doesn't matter that you never agreed to be a beta tester for them; you get to do it anyway.- Pro Writing Aid actually counts the occurrences of words in your document and tells you when a word has been overused compared to published literature. Grammarly, on the other hand, seems hell-bent to remove certain words that it has deemed overused from the language, whether or not they're actually overused in your document.- Grammarly's Clarity function is simply horrible. It mangles sentences and changes their meaning. Sometimes the result of its suggestion is unintelligible garbage.- Grammarly allows you to turn off some checks, but not all of them. Unfortunately, the ones you cannot turn off are some of the most irritating (such as that horrible "Clarity"). On the other hand, Pro Writing Aid lets you choose which checks you use.- Pro Writing Aid has a mediocre command of American English (it's a British product). The app insists on rules of grammar and spelling that are outright wrong, per Merriam-Webster, the Chicago Manual of Style, and modern usage as shown by Google Books Ngram. At one point, Pro Writing Aid insisted that American English did not include the words "holiday" and "autumn," that "vacation" and "fall" must be used instead.- Pro Writing Aid's rules for commas are 100 percent consistent with the way I learned them in high school--50 years ago! They do not reflect modern usage. Grammarly is much better at this.- Pro Writing Aid seems to waste their limited resources on tweaking their UI. Their UI most definitely could use improvement, but these changes are not great improvements; they only serve to confuse users. Their resources would be better spent fixing the many functional problems in their app.- Some of Pro Writing Aid's checks are completely useless, as they do not take context into consideration. For example, an ordinary word would not be capitalized as part of a narrative, but would be as part of a title (for example, "professor." But if you capitalize correctly for context, Pro Writing Aid dings you for "Inconsistent capitalization." Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.

#9665. How to Convert an Image to Base64 in JavaScript (3 Ways)

Posted on Nov 17 • Originally published at toolstead.net

There are three common ways to turn an image into Base64 in a browser, and they are not interchangeable. Two of them preserve your bytes exactly and one quietly re-encodes the image; one of them cannot be used on a file the user has not chosen; and on large files one of them will blow the call stack if you write it the obvious way.

Here is what each one actually does, and when to reach for it.

If you want the exact bytes of the file the user selected — no re-compression, no metadata loss — FileReader.readAsDataURL is the tool. It reads the file, Base64-encodes it, and hands you a complete data URI including the prefix.

Note what reader.result contains: the whole data URI, prefix included. If your API expects only the payload, split on the first comma — and be aware that the declared type comes from the file's type property, which is derived from the extension and can be wrong. For an API, it is worth verifying the signature against the bytes.

FileReader streams the file rather than materialising it as an array first, so it is the friendliest of the three to memory. It accepts Blob and File objects, which means it also works on data you generated yourself:

canvas.toDataURL() re-encodes the image through the browser's own encoder. That is what you want if you are resizing, cropping, or normalising a format — and exactly what you must avoid if you care about the original file.

Four consequences worth knowing before you use it:

Alpha matters here too: converting a transparent PNG to image/jpeg fills transparency with black, because JPEG has no alpha channel.

Sometimes you want the Base64 payload on its own, or you want to build the data URI yourself so you control the declared type. Read the file as an array buffer and encode it:

The naive implementation of that last step is where people get burned:

String.fromCharCode(...bytes) spreads every byte into an argument list, and argument lists have a length limit — in practice around 65,535 in most engines. On a 200 KB image you get RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded, which reads like a recursion bug and is actually an argument-count limit.

The fix is to process the buffer in chunks:

Two more details that only show up with real data. First, btoa operates on code units, not bytes — feeding it a string that contains anything above 0x7F throws InvalidCharacterError, which is why the byte-to-string step above uses fromCharCode on raw bytes rather than on decoded text. Second, the reverse direction has the same trap in mirror image: Uint8Array.from(atob(s), c => c.charCodeAt(0)) is correct, while treating the result of atob as text and passing it to a Blob corrupts every byte above 0x7F.

Base64 output is about 1.37 times the size of the input bytes, and in JavaScript that string is stored as UTF-16 — two bytes per character. The multiplication is worth doing once, because it explains why "just convert it in the browser" stops working at a certain file size:

Add the original buffer, which you are usually still holding, and a 10 MB image costs roughly 37 MB at the moment of conversion. That is survivable on a desktop and uncomfortable on a phone, which is why the encode side of our tool accepts images up to 100 MB for previewing but keeps the generated string out of the DOM — a textarea holding 137 MB of UTF-16 is the specific failure mode that makes mobile browsers kill the tab.

If you must handle very large images, process them as blobs and never build the whole string: upload the Blob directly, or stream it in chunks and encode each chunk separately. Base64 is convenient precisely because it is text, and text is the expensive representation.

The prefix is a claim, and different consumers want different shapes. A CSS url() needs the full data URI in quotes; an needs the same string; a JSON API usually wants the bare payload plus a separate content type; an email template often wants the payload wrapped at 76 characters per line. Our Image to Base64 tool exists mainly to produce those variants — including URL-safe output, line-wrapped output, and the surrounding quotes — because getting the wrapper wrong is a more common failure than getting the encoding wrong. If you are generating the string in code, write a test that decodes your own output and compares it byte for byte with the input; that single assertion catches every wrapper mistake listed above.

It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown! Only this version comes in cake form. The decoration is deceptively easy: Stack two small Bundts, frost the entire thing, and add a chocolate-dipped ice cream cone for the stem.
