#9633. Claude Code vs Codex vs Gemini CLI vs Hermes: the October 2026 comparison

Posted on Nov 17 • Originally published at colombani.ai • AI-assisted

Codex vs Claude Code vs Gemini CLI? Claude Code suits an engineering team that wants the most built-in controls, Codex an organisation already on ChatGPT, and Gemini CLI a company equipped with Gemini Code Assist. All three read your repository, edit code and run commands.

What is the Google equivalent of Codex? Antigravity CLI for an individual, free with a Google account or included in Google AI Pro and Ultra. In a company, Gemini CLI remains available with a Code Assist licence, a paid API key or Vertex AI.

A command-line (CLI) coding agent reads your repository, edits files and runs commands in your terminal until the task is done.

Four vendors lead the field in October 2026: Anthropic with Claude Code, OpenAI with Codex, Google with Gemini CLI and its consumer successor Antigravity CLI, and NousResearch with Hermes Agent. OpenClaw completes the picture on the community side.

This comparison draws on months of use in real repositories. There is no absolute ranking: the best tool depends on your team, your budget and your data constraints.

Claude Code is our default recommendation for an engineering team: Opus 5.5 on every plan, hooks, skills, per-tool approvals and a classifier-based auto mode. Codex is the natural pick for an organisation already on ChatGPT: it is included in every plan and its code is open. At Google, the answer depends on the account: Antigravity CLI for an individual, Gemini CLI for a company. Hermes Agent suits one person who wants a multi-model agent that learns from their sessions.

Prices come from the vendors' official pages, in US dollars before tax, checked on October 16, 2026.

Rolling out a coding agent to a team? Colombani.ai trains developers on the tool you choose: our Claude Code training, two days on your repositories, or Codex for teams already on ChatGPT.

The facts that changed this comparison since September, checked against the vendors' changelogs and pricing pages.

The verdict rests on repeated use in real repositories rather than a one-shot benchmark. Five criteria matter in production: quality on multi-file changes, context retention, tool integration, team governance and total operating cost.

Every price, version and licence quoted here was checked on October 16, 2026 against the vendor's documentation, GitHub repository or changelog, linked at the end. Colombani.ai trains teams on Claude Code and on Codex, so readers know where the author stands.

All of these agents support MCP (Model Context Protocol), the standard protocol that lets them plug into the same external tools: databases, ticketing, documentation. The real differences lie elsewhere.

Data residency means where your requests are processed and stored. For an organisation subject to GDPR, this row often weighs more than the price.

Claude Code is the oldest CLI agent from a major vendor: its public repository dates from February 2025, two months before those of Codex and Gemini CLI.

Since version 2.1.280 (September 22, 2026), Opus 5.5 is the default model on every plan, including Pro and the Team Standard seat. Opus excels at long tasks: multi-file refactoring, subtle bug hunting, system architecture.

The agentic loop. Claude Code sends a request to the Claude API. The response includes a stop_reason: "tool_use" means the model wants to use a tool (read a file, run a command), "end_turn" means it's done. The model itself decides when to stop.

Agentic search. Anthropic abandoned the RAG approach (vector database) in favor of iterative search: Grep, Glob, Read. The model searches, refines, searches again. Slower than a vector index, but significantly more reliable on real code.

Auto mode uses classifiers that evaluate the risk of each action before executing it. Writing a test file: low risk, automatic execution. Deleting a directory: high risk, asks for confirmation.

The harness, meaning everything around the model that guides and constrains it. CLAUDE.md gives the model persistent context: coding conventions, architecture, business constraints. Since version 2.1.277 (September 18), Claude Code reads AGENTS.md when a repository has no CLAUDE.md. Skills package reusable procedures, and Hooks run a check before or after each action.

Beyond the terminal. Subagents are stable and run in the background. Agent teams, where several instances split a task, remain experimental and off by default. Routines run scheduled tasks in the cloud, and since September 17 Projects coordinate parallel sessions with shared memory.

Opus is not the top of the range. Anthropic also offers Fable, available in Claude Code through the best alias, with its own weekly limit and, depending on the plan, usage credits.

The downsides. Claude Code is not open source and has no free plan. The one million token context window is now standard on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, so the old context limitation is gone.

Codex is OpenAI's agent, written in Rust. Its code has been published under the Apache 2.0 licence since the first commit on April 16, 2025. This permissive licence allows commercial use, modification and redistribution, and expressly grants a patent licence.

Built into ChatGPT. Since July 9, 2026 (version 26.707), Codex is part of the ChatGPT desktop app on macOS and Windows. For an organisation already on ChatGPT Business or Enterprise, the coding agent is available without a new contract.

The models. GPT-6 Luna and GPT-6 Sol arrived on September 22, 2026, and GPT-6.1 Sol on September 29. GPT-5.5 was retired on October 14 for users signed in with their ChatGPT account. Sessions authenticated with an API key are not affected.

What each plan gives you. Free and Go ($8) open Codex in the desktop app with GPT-6 Luna. The CLI, the IDE extension and Codex on the web are available from the Plus plan ($20), with GPT-6.1 Sol. Pro comes at $100, $200 and $500, Business costs $20 per user billed annually or $25 monthly, and Enterprise and Edu are priced on request.

Native subagents and fast startup. Codex delegates subtasks to parallel agents. Charlie Marsh, the author of uv and ruff, rewrote its startup phase on August 20, which is now about 25 times faster. Amazon Bedrock is natively supported as a provider, useful when code must stay on infrastructure you control.

The downsides. The codex mcp-server command, which exposed Codex as an MCP server to other tools, was removed on September 5, 2026: integrations that used it must move to the app server. Usage limits depend on the plan and the model, and are best measured on the usage dashboard rather than the price list.

This question comes up constantly, and the two tools have converged: repository access, MCP, skills, subagents, hooks. Comparing their features is no longer enough to tell them apart. Three questions settle it.

Which subscription does the organisation already pay for? A company on ChatGPT Business gets Codex at no extra cost. A company on Claude Team gets Claude Code from the Standard seat. The entry price is the same: $20 a month billed annually.

What does it need to be able to verify? Codex publishes its harness code under Apache 2.0, which makes it auditable. Claude Code keeps a readable local record of what the agent saw and sent, with tool-by-tool approvals.

Who reviews the code it produces? For a team shipping to production, Claude Code with Opus 5.5 remains our default recommendation. Codex takes the lead when internal policy requires an open licence or routing through Amazon Bedrock.

The two combine well: one agent writes, the other reviews, and their blind spots differ. The detailed analysis is in Codex or Claude Code: how to choose in 2026.

For an individual: Antigravity CLI. Available to everyone, it shares its engine with Antigravity 2.0, Google's desktop app for agent-first development. It is written in Go and orchestrates several agents in the background. It keeps Gemini CLI's key features: Skills, Hooks, subagents and extensions, now called plugins.

For a company: Gemini CLI remains available. Organisations with a Gemini Code Assist Standard or Enterprise licence keep their access, as do paid API keys and Vertex AI. Version 0.64.0 (October 13, 2026) runs on the Gemini 3 family, with Gemini 3.1 Pro in preview. The repository README states that Gemini CLI has not been optimized for Gemini 4 Argon and points to Antigravity for that model.

What sets them apart. Gemini CLI stays open source under Apache 2.0. The Antigravity CLI repository only publishes documentation and the changelog. Antigravity CLI, on the other hand, offers Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 to authorised Google Cloud projects. Its auto mode sends any command that would leave the sandbox to a second agent for review.

What is no longer true. Gemini CLI is no longer "free with a Google account". The repository README now says so at the top: for the unpaid tier and Google One users, Gemini CLI was replaced by Antigravity CLI on June 18, 2026. Gemini CLI also has Skills, Hooks and subagents, contrary to what this comparison stated before October. Gemini Code Assist for GitHub has accepted no new installations since June 18, except through Google Cloud.

Antigravity CLI's free-tier quotas do not appear in the sources we checked, so we do not quote them. For Gemini on the productivity side, see Gemini for business.

Hermes Agent from NousResearch is the most original on this list. Its standout feature: a built-in learning loop. The agent creates skills from your sessions, improves them through use, and builds a persistent profile of your preferences.

NousResearch describes it as the only agent with a built-in learning loop: it adapts to its user automatically, where Claude Code requires maintaining a CLAUDE.md file by hand.

Multi-provider. Hermes works with OpenRouter, Nous Portal, OpenAI, your own endpoint or local models, and can switch models mid-session. Since 0.22.0, it installs llama.cpp and runs an open model on your machine in one click, with no account and no API key.

Multi-platform. Beyond the terminal, Hermes can be driven from a desktop app, Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp or Signal, through a single gateway.

A project that has grown considerably. Six months after its first public releases in March 2026, Hermes has around 254,000 GitHub stars as of October 16, under the MIT licence. The 0.22.0 cycle alone brought together about 2,500 contributors. Version 0.22.2 (October 15) is the latest stable release.

The downsides. The pace is still dizzying: about 24,000 commits between 0.21.0 and 0.22.0. The stable release channels introduced on October 14 reduce the risk, but pinning a version remains the rule before any client work. The learning loop can retain mistakes. And the optional GODMODE skill, which ships sample prompts for bypassing guardrails, raises a legitimate security question.

Codex is a software vendor's coding agent, tied to a ChatGPT subscription and to OpenAI models. Hermes is a provider-independent personal agent that also writes code.

Choose Codex when the agent serves a team that must share configuration, billing and administration: ChatGPT workspace, SSO, audit logs, residency controls on Enterprise.

Choose Hermes when one person wants a single agent for code, messaging and scheduled tasks, with the model of their choice, including a local one. The hermes import-agent command, added in August, imports an existing Codex or Claude Code setup.

Both licences are permissive: Apache 2.0 for Codex, MIT for Hermes. The difference is governance: Codex is administered like an enterprise service, while Hermes is self-hosted and secured by its user.

OpenClaw (ex-Clawdbot, ex-Moltbot) has the most chaotic trajectory of the bunch: renamed twice after an Anthropic trademark complaint, 60,000 GitHub stars in 72 hours at launch, around 392,000 as of October 16, 2026, and its creator, Peter Steinberger, hired by OpenAI.

Persistent local memory. This feature is what made it a success. OpenClaw remembers your sessions for weeks, with no configuration.

Works with several models. It runs with Claude, GPT or open models such as Kimi.

More than a coding agent. OpenClaw positions itself as a "Life OS": WhatsApp connection, calendar management, third-party app control. The most ambitious approach, and the riskiest.

The downsides. Security. 923 OpenClaw gateways were recorded as exposed without authentication, with shell access and API keys in plain text. If you deploy OpenClaw, lock it down before any use: our AI agent security course covers isolation, permissions and exfiltration through agent tools.

GitHub Copilot CLI requires an active Copilot subscription and can be disabled by the organisation's administrator (version 1.0.99, October 16). OpenCode is an open source, multi-model agent under the MIT licence, with around 214,000 stars (version 1.19.1, October 15). Amp runs its agents remotely: they keep working after you close your laptop. Cursor CLI brings Cursor's agent to the terminal, with models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Cursor.

Already deploying agents in production? Beyond the tool, two turnkey offerings:

Here are our recommendations by use case.

Demanding solo developer: Claude Code. Opus 5.5 by default from the Pro plan makes the difference when every mistake costs you time. Alternative: Antigravity CLI to get started with a Google account.

Structured engineering team: Claude Code. Shared CLAUDE.md in Git, Hooks to enforce conventions, worktrees for parallel work. The investment in the harness pays off once the team exceeds two or three people.

Organisation already on ChatGPT Business or Enterprise: Codex. The agent is included, so is the administration, and the Apache 2.0 licence makes the harness auditable.

Company on Google Cloud: Gemini CLI with a Code Assist licence, or Antigravity CLI attached to your Google Cloud projects.

Enterprise or mid-size company: Claude Code. Governance (Skills, security Hooks, permissions) and the tool's track record meet the requirements of structured teams. Before a company-wide rollout, an enterprise AI maturity audit shows what can be tested now and what must be prepared.

Team building its own agents: once the coding agent is mastered, the MCP and Agent SDK training teaches how to design, evaluate and run custom agents, with their MCP servers. Architects who want that skill attested can follow our preparation for the Claude Certified Architect certification, issued by Anthropic.

Student or learner: Antigravity CLI with a Google account, or Codex in the ChatGPT app from the free plan.

Open source contributor: Codex, Gemini CLI, Hermes Agent or OpenCode, all published under open licences.

Multi-model experimentation: Hermes Agent. Mid-session model switching and one-click local models make it easy to compare LLMs on the same project.

Power user: OpenClaw. Persistent memory and the multi-platform approach are unique. Secure your installation.

Business teams who do not code: these command-line agents are not the right entry point; the AI agents training for companies runs on the tool already in place, with no terminal; for an organisation on ChatGPT, the ChatGPT training for companies follows the same approach.

To roll out one of these agents to a team, Colombani.ai offers two courses: Claude Code in production and Codex.

At Colombani.ai, we train first on Claude Code, because it brings together the most complete set of tools: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Hooks, per-tool approvals and a classifier-based auto mode. We also train on Codex for teams that work in ChatGPT.

Every training shows the alternatives, because methodology matters as much as the tool. Structuring your context, planning before coding, verifying systematically: these principles work with any agent.

A well-written CLAUDE.md is a project conventions document, and Claude Code now reads AGENTS.md, the format Codex also uses. Skills exist at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. The discipline of verification (tests, diff review) is universal.

The field moves fast: Google replaced its consumer agent within a month, OpenAI changed models twice in one week, and Hermes passed 250,000 stars in six months. A structured method for coding with AI keeps all its value.

Once the tool is chosen, the Claude Code in production or Codex course gets your team to adopt the method, on your own repositories.

Ulysse Trin is the founder of Colombani.ai, an AI consulting and training firm based in Paris. This article first appeared on the Colombani.ai blog.

#9631. The Flaw Chipmakers Spent 50 Years Fighting Is Now Their Best Feature: Memory Chip Fingerprinting

A cybersecurity researcher and enthusiast who likes to get to the bottom of niche topics and share the information found with the public.

A cybersecurity researcher and enthusiast who likes to get to the bottom of niche topics and share the information found with the public.

A cybersecurity researcher and enthusiast who likes to get to the bottom of niche topics and share the information found with the public.

Memory chips of the same model, with identical serial numbers and the same price, come off the manufacturing line. But when they are powered on, each begins its unique pattern of making tiny mistakes. For years, these mistakes were a target for the engineers trying to eliminate them. However, security specialists found ways to use them for anti-counterfeit protection, securing encryption keys, and even tracing people.

The ideal memory chip should be fast, cheap, spacious, and non-volatile. None exist. Hence, computers use different types of memory chips, each of them having some advantages in particular tasks.

SRAM uses the miniature closed circuit of transistors containing two possible states for every bit - like a light switch. It is the fastest memory but requires six transistors to store one bit and, therefore, is expensive and big. SRAM is used in the cache memory and microcontrollers' memory.

DRAM stores each bit in the form of the amount of charge in the capacitor. Only one transistor and a capacitor are necessary to store one bit. Therefore, it is cheap and small enough to become the primary memory of the computer. Unfortunately, the charge stored in it leaks away with time, and the memory needs refreshing every 64 milliseconds.

Flash uses a special transistor in which the charge is trapped in the insulator. Once in there, electrons remain trapped for years, making flash a good choice for phone memory, SSDs, and USB drives. The writing and erasing process of the flash is slower than that of other memories, as erasure happens in blocks. Additionally, the erasure process damages the insulator, hence limiting the usage of the memory in several thousands of erasing cycles.

Modern chip factories work with technologies on an atomic level, and atoms rarely fall in place identically each time. Therefore, one transistor may be slightly stronger than its neighbour, one capacitor - leakier, some insulator layers - thinner. The manufacturers try to hide those defects under the safe margins and make all memory chips behave alike. However, if pushed to the very limit of these margins, individual flaws will start causing flipped bits.

For instance, when an SRAM chip is powered on, it does not know what its starting state is. Powering on a cell means letting it choose the desirable state, and it always depends on which of the two sides wins, the winning side being a bit stronger.

For DRAM, if it is disturbed somehow, it will forget its contents. Without refreshing the memory, the leakiest cells will forget their contents first. Moreover, in DRAM, there is a more serious flaw: the reading of some rows of the memory will affect the adjacent rows, flipping the bits in the memory that was not accessed by the program. This is the infamous Rowhammer effect. In 2014, researchers detected it in 110 out of 129 memory modules they tested.

As with DRAM, in flash memory, changing the content of one cell can affect the state of the neighbouring cells. Besides, the cells of flash memory wear out differently: some of them can be programmed after only a few writing cycles, whilst some will require many more of them.

Now that we know the flaws of each memory type, we can force errors and pinpoint their location. This pattern of errors is different in each chip but unique to one particular chip, just like a fingerprint. Researchers call it a physical unclonable function since even the manufacturer will not be able to create another chip with the same fingerprint pattern.

Turn on an SRAM chip and read its content right after. Most of the cells wake up identically each time, creating the long series of ones and zeros that are unique to this one chip. Comparison of two power-ups of the same chip shows that differences occur in fewer than ten per cent of the bits. On the contrary, comparing two different chips shows differences in about half of the bits. This makes it possible to identify each chip reliably.

For DRAM chips, the easiest way is to write some pattern into the memory, interrupt its refresh, and see which cells forget the content. The set of forgetful cells is a fingerprint. This method works without any additional hardware but takes minutes. A more sophisticated way is to read the memory with deliberately quick timing, and the cells that cannot cope will show up in about 88 milliseconds.

Rowhammer provides another approach. In a study done in 2025, about a hundred memory modules were hammered, and the fingerprints distinguished between chips with 99.91% accuracy in less than five seconds.

For flash, under normal operation, a flash memory chip continues pulsing the cell until its contents are safely stored. Fingerprinting involves stopping this process halfway. Apply the same number of short pulses to all the cells and stop - some fast cells will be ready, but the slow ones will still be blank. This pattern of fast and slow cells becomes the unique fingerprint of a chip. The opposite technique of stopping an erase halfway through works in the reverse direction and even for the flash memory integrated into everyday microcontrollers. Everything happens using the usual chip interface, without any special equipment.

Those fingerprints can be used as keys that are never stored on the chip. If a secret key is stored in a chip, it can be recovered by an attacker. However, the key derived from the chip fingerprint is different. It is generated each time the device is powered on with error correction, and it vanishes when the power goes off. There is nothing to steal from the powered-off device.

Another useful application is proving the identity. Manufacturers record the fingerprints of each chip in the factory. Then the server challenges the device to reproduce its fingerprint. This way, even affordable sensors and smart tags get a strong identity without additional security chips.

Similarly, counterfeit and recycled components can be detected. Used chips from electronic waste are regularly sold as new. Fingerprint verification will detect a chip not registered by the legitimate manufacturer, whilst analysis of the flash memory will provide even more information. Since the erasure operations take more time with ageing of the memory cells, the time it takes to execute these operations alone will indicate the remaining service life of the microchip.

And finally, random numbers. The cells that fail to settle in the single state have another useful property - they generate true random numbers, which are always needed by cryptography.

However, despite having many useful applications, hardware fingerprints can also be used to track devices, and not always for good purposes. The fingerprint that cannot be changed is a fingerprint that cannot be hidden. One study showed that energy-efficient memory that tolerates minor errors produces enough errors to identify the machine that created a file. Moreover, extracting fingerprints is hard on hardware: Rowhammer attacks damage data, and flash-based approaches consume a part of the chip's lifespan.

However, the main idea of all this remains quite positive. Flaws that engineers tried to eliminate during fifty years turned out to be one of the most reliable features of the chip - the identity based on physics, chosen by no one and impossible to copy.

A cybersecurity researcher and enthusiast who likes to get to the bottom of niche topics and share the information found with the public.

#9630. 16 pumpkin recipes, from cakes and cookies to bars and bread: We've got a marbled pumpkin cake, chewy pumpkin cookies, and even pumpkin milk bread.

It’s that time of year when pumpkin spice everything starts appearing on store shelves — candles, lip balm, air fresheners, beer, and of course, the ubiquitous PSL (pumpkin spice latte). That means fall is here, and more importantly, that pumpkin should make a grand return to your kitchen! Pull out your canned pumpkin — or better yet, make your own pumpkin purée — and stock your pantry with pumpkin pie spice, because we have the best pumpkin recipes to bake this fall.

This Pumpkin Swirl Cake takes my breath away every time I unmold it from its intricate loaf pan. The anticipation keeps building until I slice into the pound cake-like loaf and reveal the swirled pattern inside, marbled with both vanilla and spiced pumpkin batter. (Don’t fret if you don’t have the specialty loaf pan — this can also be baked in a standard loaf pan and adorned with a simple confectioners’ sugar icing.)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Patch O Pumpkins Loaf Pan and Pure Vanilla Plus

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Sparkling Sugar

A cousin of Belgian-style Liège waffles, these Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles have caramelized edges and a pleasant chew that’s reminiscent of brioche. The yeasted batter has pumpkin in it for flavor and color, plus Swedish pearl sugar that melts into pockets of crispy sugar. The best part? The batter rests overnight, so if you prepare it the night ahead, all you have to do the next morning is scoop and cook the batter for hot, crispy waffles in just a few minutes.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles

To make this recipe, you'll need: Swedish Pearl Sugar

I used to make the same pumpkin pie recipe for years, and it always left me wanting a little more excitement. Then I found this Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie and never looked back! The generously spiced filling uses nutmeg, ginger, cloves, and Vietnamese cinnamon to create a more flavorful pie than traditional versions. The secret to its silky-smooth texture? Corn syrup, which is an invert sugar and keeps the custard from becoming grainy. Substitute another invert sugar like honey or maple syrup if you like; I use maple syrup.

Get the recipe: Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon, Ginger, and Nutmeg

Whenever I have these tender, golden scones on hand, I look forward to getting out of bed the next morning because I know they’re waiting for me. They can be easily customized to use a range of mix-ins, depending on what you have in your pantry. My personal preference is a mix of crystallized ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits.

Get the recipe: Harvest Pumpkin Scones (or Gluten-Free Pumpkin Scones)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Mini Diced Ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits

If you’re looking for a way to make your whole kitchen smell like fall, these one-bowl, easy pumpkin muffins deliver — and fast. They’re ready in under an hour, so you can spend less time measuring, mixing, and cleaning and more time tackling your autumn bucket list.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Standard Muffin Pan

Making banana bread is an almost weekly activity in my house — except during fall, when we pivot to pumpkin bread instead. This is a quick, easy bake that satisfies my craving for something pumpkin-y, and it uses a simple trick to concentrate the pumpkin flavor and ensure the loaf is perfectly textured: The pumpkin purée is reduced on the stovetop to cook off excess moisture. (The process is similar to browning butter.) As a result, the final loaf is packed with pumpkin flavor.

Get the recipe: The Most Pumpkin Pumpkin Chocolate Chip Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: Ginger and Semisweet Chocolate Chips

These bars have all the cozy, spiced goodness of the classic dessert in a portable, crowd-friendly form. The buttery, brown sugar crust gets pressed into the pan (no rolling out pie dough!), and the silky pumpkin filling comes together with just a handful of ingredients. The (optional but highly recommended) sour cream whipped topping brings a slight tanginess and completes the traditional pumpkin pie experience.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This Pumpkin Milk Bread is exceptionally soft, squishy, and feather-light, while also packing in a lot of pumpkin. Pumpkin can often weigh down baked goods, but here the combination of a tangzhong, bread flour, and a long mix makes this bread simultaneously moist and high-rising.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant Yeast

This tender pumpkin crumb cake is for people who double the chocolate chips in pumpkin bread and the streusel on coffee cake. Atop the thin layer of spiced pumpkin cake lays a heavy blanket of buttery crumbs with a bold chocolate flavor, thanks to Dutch-processed cocoa powder.

Get the recipe: Chocolate-Pumpkin Crumb Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Black Cocoa

These Pumpkin Cupcakes, with their piped swirl of cream cheese frosting, are the ideal way to celebrate fall birthdays. The cupcakes are super tender, thanks to the addition of cake flour and oil. Sour cream and brown sugar add tanginess and molasses-y sweetness while also preventing the cupcakes from being dry.

For more cupcake decorating ideas, see our YouTube video: Decorate Cupcakes Better Than Ever.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Cake Flour (or Gluten-Free Measure for Measure Flour)

My husband’s favorite fall dessert is Pumpkin Whoopie Pies, hands down. He can’t resist these subtly sweet cakes sandwiching rich cream cheese filling. This recipe has a few extra bells and whistles to take it over the top: Bread and Cake Enhancer to keep the cakes extra soft and fresh, xanthan gum in the filling to give it a smooth mouthfeel, and diced crystallized ginger for a bit of extra zing in the filling.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Bread and Cake Enhancer, Xanthan Gum, and Mini Diced Ginger

The next time there’s a rainy weekend, I’m taking on a project bake: our Pumpkin Cream Cheese Danish. It’s a multiday process and laminating dough is a labor of love, but the final product is worth the effort: buttery, crisp pastries filled with pumpkin and sweet cream cheese.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Cream Cheese Danish

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting is a show-stopping dessert featuring spiced layers of cake, not-too-sweet cream cheese frosting, and a blanket of melted caramel poured over the top. Will it be slightly messy to serve? Yes. Will anyone mind? Absolutely not.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Offset Spatula

The pumpkin spice recipe I’m most excited to bake this fall is a mash-up of greats: Part-coffee cake, part-Bundt cake, part-pumpkin bread, this Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake deserves a category all of its own. It has two layers of espresso swirl tucked within a moist, spiced cake. Make it in your favorite Bundt pan or serve it as a loaf if you’re more of simple-is-better person. Either way, it’s great for snacking all day long.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Espresso Powder and Bundt Pan

#9629. How to Ask Wabi to Build the Mini-App You Actually Want: A 4-Part Prompt Formula

I'm the author of Wabi Wiki, an unofficial guide to the Wabi AI assistant — not affiliated with Wabi. The examples below come from the guide's prompts library.

Wabi's party trick is simple to describe and easy to get wrong: you describe what you want in plain language, and it builds a small app inside your chat — a poll, a tracker, a shared list, a quiz. But because Wabi generates each app fresh from your description, a vague request gives you a vague app. After collecting the prompts that work best, the pattern comes down to four parts.

"Build a poll" beats "plan my whole wedding." Wabi does best when each message asks for one thing: one poll, one tracker, one list. If your request has three jobs in it, split it into three messages. You will get three working tools instead of one confused one.

Wabi's specialty is group apps, so name the people. "Make a poll so our group can vote on one of these five movies for Friday night" works because it says who votes and what they are choosing. "Quiz my daughter on Japanese vocabulary for 10 minutes, three times a week" works because it names the person, the subject, the length and the schedule. A request with no audience gets a generic app; a request with a named audience gets one that fits.

If you will check something daily, say so — and ask for a home-screen widget. "Create a countdown to our trip on June 5 and put it on my home screen" tells Wabi both the job and the place. The same goes for check-ins: "Create a habit tracker that fits my morning routine and checks in with me daily" sets the rhythm up front instead of leaving Wabi to guess.

Your first version is a draft, not a verdict. Ask Wabi to add a field, change a reminder time, or share the app with the thread. Each small fix keeps everything that already worked. Starting over from scratch throws away the good parts along with the bad.

Each better version follows the formula: one tool, named people, a place or rhythm, and room to refine.

Pick one small job — a shared list, a poll, a tracker — and write the request with all four parts before you send it. If the result is close but not right, change one thing and ask again. You can find the full prompts library with copy-paste examples for trips, family, health and daily life at Wabi Wiki.

#9625. Trybit Upgrades Crypto Infrastructure with New API and Interface for High-Volume Mass Payouts

Your Trusted Crypto & Blockchain Newswire

Your Trusted Crypto & Blockchain Newswire

Your Trusted Crypto & Blockchain Newswire

Panama, November,11 — Trybit, a global crypto payment gateway for online businesses, has released a new mass payout workflow with a new interface and API. The update adds a step-by-step form for creating mass payouts, line-by-line validation before submission, an individual status for each recipient and a searchable payout history. Trybit has also improved notifications in the personal account and added new account emails.

Sending one crypto transfer is simple. Sending hundreds at once is where things go wrong. One mistyped address in a long list can hold up the whole mass payout or send funds where they cannot be recovered. When part of a mass payout goes through and part does not, finance teams have to work out by hand who was paid. Re-sending without that answer risks paying the same person twice.

Marketplaces, affiliate programs, gaming platforms and companies with remote contractors face this every payout cycle. Many of them still reconcile crypto payouts in spreadsheets.

Mass payouts are now created through a step-by-step form with three ways to add recipients:

A Download template button gives teams a template that matches the format the system accepts: recipient address, amount and, if needed, currency. Teams no longer have to build the file from the format description in the documentation. The network for each recipient is detected automatically from the address, so nobody has to select it line by line.

A file is more practical for regular payouts, when the list is exported from accounting software. For fully automated workflows, mass payouts via API remain available.

Every line in the recipient list is checked before the payout is submitted for processing. If a line has a problem, the error is shown next to that specific line. A team fixes the one entry that needs attention instead of rebuilding the whole file or finding the mistake after the money is gone. For cryptocurrency payouts, this is essential: a transfer to the wrong address cannot be reversed, and the check before funds are debited is the only point at which an error can be corrected without loss.

Once the mass payout is sent, each line in the list shows its own status. If most transfers go through and a few do not, the team sees exactly which ones need attention. Reconciliation becomes a check of one screen instead of comparing wallet history against a spreadsheet. A summary of each mass payout is also sent by email.

Sent mass payouts are saved to the history, which supports search and status filters. This makes it faster to answer a partner who asks whether a payout was sent, and to pull records together for an audit.

The update also changes how teams learn about account events. All events now come through a single notification feed in the personal account, with new notification types for partial invoice payments, exchanges and errors. Notifications have a dedicated page: events are grouped by day, the category filter shows a count for each category, and important notifications can be pinned. The feed updates in real time, with no need to reload the page.

All emails are now sent through a single mechanism that prevents duplicates and limits sending frequency, so the same event no longer reaches the inbox twice. New emails cover withdrawal completion, mass payout summaries, failed AML checks and more.

The new API mirrors the interface, so teams that run payouts from their own back end get the same workflow without opening the personal account. Through the API, a team can submit a mass payout built from a file or a recipient list, receive validation errors for specific lines before anything is sent, track the status of each transfer and look up the payout history. Payouts are authorized with a dedicated payout API key, generated in the Security section of the account settings and separate from the project's main API key. API payouts can go to any address, including addresses that are not on the account's saved list.

API reference: docs.trybit.com/api-reference-v2/withdrawals.

The interface works on desktop and tablets and is available in Spanish and Portuguese, among other languages.

Trybit  is a global crypto payment gateway built for high-volume online platforms that accept and pay out in the most popular crypto currencies and stablecoins. It applies AML/KYT screening of incoming transactions before crediting to the merchant’s balance. The rest of the payment cycle covers automatic conversion into stablecoins, mass payouts, static wallets, CMS integrations, and White Label (Host2Host) options for platforms that want the payment flow under their own brand.

#9623. IronWallet Review: A Simple, Open Wallet That Is Growing Fast

Your Trusted Crypto & Blockchain Newswire

Your Trusted Crypto & Blockchain Newswire

Your Trusted Crypto & Blockchain Newswire

IronWallet seems to have appeared out of nowhere, but according to Ermo Eero, the project has been around for four and a half years. The idea was to build a simple, easy-to-use crypto wallet that anyone can open, with no KYC, no ID checks, and no sign-ups. What started as a niche project has grown into a competitive product. Its most notable feature is gasless transfers, which let users move funds without holding the network's native coin to pay fees. IronWallet also offers gasless swaps, routed through SwapKit, one of the market's leading swap aggregators.

IronWallet comes across as a solid all-rounder. Everything runs inside the app: sending, receiving, swapping, and buying crypto. Everything seemed to work well. Buying requires some form of KYC, which is expected, but the choice of payment providers offered in the app was wider than I anticipated.

The biggest gap is network coverage. IronWallet supports 12 networks. They include many of the most popular chains, but established non-custodial wallets support considerably more, and IronWallet still has ground to make up against the market leaders.

The second gap is platform. There is no desktop or web version. Nearly every competitor offers one, and for users who manage funds from a computer, that is a real limitation.

IronWallet's answer to that gap is its MCP server. The MCP is open source, and it works somewhat like a desktop companion: it lets AI agents in desktop tools control the wallet, and it includes a local wallet manager that opens in your own browser for adding, importing, backing up, and deleting wallets. Experienced users of desktop AI agents will likely find it straightforward to set up. For newcomers, the advice is simple: read the FAQ first.

IronWallet is a clear, open, and easy-to-use non-custodial wallet, and it is improving quickly. Its gasless transfers and gasless swaps make everyday use simpler, and buying crypto inside the app is a practical bonus. Network count and platform reach are the areas to watch, and with a project that has been building steadily for years, the momentum suggests they will keep improving. For mobile users who value simplicity and no-KYC access, IronWallet is already a strong choice, and it is well worth a look.

#9622. What are flour enzymes?: Understanding a common flour ingredient.

If you look closely at a bag of King Arthur flour, you may see an unfamiliar ingredient listed there: enzyme.

We’re extremely thoughtful about every ingredient we use, across all King Arthur products and recipes. Our Food Philosophy guides every decision to ensure the quality of what we create, and that includes the enzymes in our flour.

Here’s exactly what flour enzymes are and why they’re included in flour.

Enzymes are found naturally in wheat, and thus are already present in flour. An enzyme is a protein produced by a living organism that acts as a catalyst to bring about a specific biochemical reaction.

The amount of enzymes in flour can vary based on growing conditions from harvest to harvest and year to year, so we add natural enzymes to correct for any variance and make sure our flour bakes more consistently — in other words, to make your baking even better. Those enzymes make up a very small portion of the total flour: less than 1%.

The enzyme we use in our flour is technically called fungal alpha-amylase. That’s a pretty technical name, so it is commonly labeled simply as “enzyme” on ingredient labels. “Alpha-amylase” is the actual enzyme, and “fungal” refers to the fact that the living organism that produces the enzyme is a fungus, not unlike yeast or a mushroom. Amylase may sound unfamiliar, but your body makes and uses it every day. When you eat, it begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates so you can draw on it for energy. Amylases added to flour perform a similar function.

Note: Though fungi are technically living organisms, enzymes are considered vegan, as they are not animal based.

Malted barley is an alternative source of enzymes that King Arthur has used in the past, but we found the efficacy can vary batch to batch. By swapping malted barley for straight enzymes, the flour produces more consistent results for our bakers.

Another reason we made the switch? Enzymes require less water and energy to produce than malt barley. As a Certified B Corporation, we're committed to being good stewards of our planet, so pivoting to a responsibly sourced ingredient with a smaller environmental footprint makes sense.

To put it simply, enzymes are added to flours to improve baking performance — they do not change the flour's nutritional value. More specifically, they help create the foods that feeds yeasts. The enzymes break down complex starches into simpler sugars; this, in turn, provides yeast with readily available fermentable sugar (food!), which enables yeast to work continuously and supports both fermentation and crust browning. This results in improved bread volume and crumb texture. Most other manufacturers of flour and yeasted mixes use enzymes for the very same reasons.

Ultimately, enzymes are yet another way for us to provide you with the most consistent flour — which means even better baking.

#9617. Give Grilled Cheese A Major Flavor And Protein Boost With One Hearty Addition

There are seemingly as many kinds of grilled cheese as there are individuals on this planet. There are, for example, plenty of international styles worth trying, while even the classic all-American versions can consist of a variety of cheeses, like American, cheddar, Gouda, and Havarti. You might like to make yours using mayonnaise on the bread, while your neighbor prefers butter in the pan. And then there are extra fillings and additions. Some people add a little bacon and maple syrup to their sandwiches, while others turn theirs into a breakfast masterpiece with an egg. Another fantastically tasty option is to add chili, which not only imbues the meal with a huge dose of extra flavor, but also gives you a nice protein boost.

Whether you have more leftover chili than you know what to do with, or a can or two in your pantry collecting dust, it's actually the perfect addition. It's savory, hearty, and saucy, which works so well when layered with cheese (which chili often gets topped with) and sandwiched between two slices of bread, pan-browned to crispy perfection. And if you have daily protein goals, a ¼ cup of chili, which is a reasonable starting quantity for a single sandwich, can typically get you roughly 4 to 5 grams closer to meeting that target (though this will vary depending on the recipe).

One of the best things about chili grilled cheese sandwiches is how easy they are to make. You can assemble them in the pan like normal, but add a scoop of chili onto one slice of bread before closing it up. This works well if you're just making one or two sandwiches, but if you have more mouths to feed, you can actually make a whole bunch in the oven at once. You'll just want to be sure to spread butter on the outside of each slice of bread, combine your chili with plenty of shredded cheese to make a gooey, melty filling, and then flip the sandwiches halfway through baking so both sides get nice and toasty.

Now, like all grilled cheeses, this variation is still quite customizable. For example, if you wanted to add some sharpness to help cut through all the richness of the other ingredients, you could sprinkle green onion on top of the chili. Alternatively, if you wanted a bite, plus a bit of spice, sliced or chopped jalapeños would do nicely (or you might make the sweet pickled version known as cowboy candy). To amp up the protein even more, some bacon wouldn't be out of place, either. You could also lean into the idea of a chili cheese dog grilled cheese, and slice a hot dog lengthwise, fry it up, and place that on top of the chili layer.

#9616. Heavy cream vs. whipping cream: What's the difference?: Understanding the right cream for your baking.

If you’re baking a recipe that calls for heavy cream, or picking up a carton to turn into whipped cream to finish a dessert, you may be confused when you hit the dairy aisle. There’s “heavy cream” — but also “heavy whipping cream” or, in some cases, just “whipping cream.”

So when it comes to heavy cream versus whipping cream, is there truly a difference?

Aside from being delicious, there are very specific definitions and standards that must be met in order for something to be labeled as heavy cream. It is made by separating the fatty top layer from the base milk layer during processing. The FDA states that heavy cream is cream that contains no less than 36% milk fat.  Comparatively, milk has 0% to around 3% milk fat, as well as a higher water concentration. Because of its fat content, heavy cream retains a rich taste and, when whipped, it excels at creating stiff peaks that hold their shape for a long time.

Whipping cream — sometimes called “heavy whipping cream” — is made using a similar process as heavy cream and is also the milk fat removed before milk is homogenized. However, whipping cream can contain somewhere between 30% and 35% milk fat content, according to FDA regulations. Because of its slightly lower fat content, it whips into a softer, more billowy cream, and it will deflate more quickly than whipped cream made with heavy cream.

Luckily, the difference in taste and performance between the two types of cream are not very discernible. This means you can use them interchangeably in recipes — and it's okay if you accidentally buy the "wrong" one. Both can yield a delicious bowl of homemade whipped cream. (Can’t justify buying a whole carton of either one? We’ve got you covered with an easy homemade heavy cream substitute.)

A note on King Arthur recipes: The King Arthur Test Kitchen prefers heavy cream in most instances, particularly when making whipped cream, because of the higher fat content. That said, you can substitute heavy whipping cream 1:1 in any King Arthur recipe that calls specifically for heavy cream without any issue.

As a general rule of thumb, use heavy cream for making stable whipped cream for topping pies, layered desserts like tiramisu or banana pudding, and any sweet where the structural integrity hinges on the cream really holding its shape. Heavy cream can also be handy for making cream scones and drop biscuits, where the richness of the dairy can shine through. For more heavy cream baking inspiration, check out these 12 recipes that call on heavy cream.

#9613. Skip Butter And Milk: The Canned Ingredient That Makes Burgers Juicier

Juicy burger patties are all about nailing the perfect ratio of fat, moisture, and protein for something that isn't wet or greasy but also isn't dry and crumbly. While butter and milk can certainly help, condensed cream of mushroom soup is a far better and easier alternative that perfectly strikes the balance when you use the right amount.

Cream of mushroom soup may be billed as a shelf-stable meal in its own right, but the condensed version is a canned soup hack for many recipes thanks to its texture and flavor. It's had much of its moisture removed and therefore has a higher ratio of fat. While wet enough to infuse proteins with a bit of juiciness, its fat content helps preserve the tenderness and protect the existing moisture, all with the delicious umami of mushrooms. Condensed varieties also tend to be more potent, so the small amount you'll use for juiciness translates into a subdued but still noticeable taste.

Chopped mushrooms for extra-juicy burgers is an increasingly common tactic, but evenly mixing all the little bits without overworking the meat is challenging. While wet ingredients are far easier to thoroughly disperse, they come with a caveat. You need a starch to hold and release the moisture unless you want it to drip out right away. Breadcrumbs are a common choice in meatballs and other ground beef recipes, and a ratio of half a cup of starch to one 10.5-ounce can to one pound of protein gets the job done quite well.

Burger patties made with condensed cream of mushroom soup are pretty forgiving and more difficult to dry out, but that doesn't mean you can just chuck them on the grill willy-nilly. To preserve the juiciness and keep them easy to work with, you need to know when to leave them alone, whether that's while they're raw, cooking, or resting.

Immediately cooking a burger infused with condensed cream of mushroom soup leaves a lot of surface moisture. This ends up steaming it, so it doesn't develop a good crust and robs it of much of the juice you were attempting to preserve. Letting any patty chill in the fridge helps it firm up and makes it easier to manipulate on the grill, but it also allows the breadcrumbs to absorb the moisture to release later. Similar to marinating, it also helps to let the flavors mix a bit, so you don't end up with pockets of intense mushroom-ness that can ruin an otherwise good bite.

While exact timing varies based on your method, the 5-6-7 rule when cooking burgers is a reliable starting point. Five minutes on one side, six on the other, then seven minutes resting helps you balance enough heat to create a crust with enough time to ensure that the insides are not still raw. The resting is particularly important, as you don't want to release all your juice onto your plate or as steam and make your subsequent bites drier.

#9608. How to clean cast iron  : It’s simpler than you think.

Despite what you may have heard, cleaning and maintaining a cast iron skillet or Dutch oven isn’t difficult. It’s practically impossible to ruin a well-seasoned skillet, and despite your best efforts, sometimes food will stick. If your cast iron is covered in stuck-on bits of cheese from a batch of Crispy Cheesy Pan Pizza, here's how to clean it.

We can settle the debate once and for all: Yes, you can use soap to clean your cast iron. Dishwashing soap will not damage the seasoning that makes your skillet non-stick. Polymerized oil creates the layer of seasoning through heat, and dish soap isn’t strong enough to break that bond.

No, you cannot clean a cast iron skillet in the dishwasher. This will degrade the seasoning layer and cause it to rust.

You should not soak a cast iron pan either; the water will cause it to rust. If you do end up rusting your pan, you can still rescue it by scrubbing off the rust then re-seasoning the pan.

Using warm, soapy water, scrub the pan with a stiff-bristled brush or sponge to remove any food residue. Avoid harsh, abrasive scrubbers like steel wool or metal pads, which can strip the pan of its seasoning.

Once cleaned, fully dry the pan with a kitchen towel, or place it onto a burner over low heat so the water fully evaporates. Don’t walk away from the pan — it can quickly get smoky once the water has evaporated.

Regardless of which method you prefer, it’s imperative that the pan is fully dry. Water (not soap!) is the enemy of cast iron, which can cause it to rust. Once dry, add a few drops of neutral oil and spread all over the pan with a towel.

#9605. Crypto ETFs: Bringing Centralization Back to Crypto?

The whole point of cryptocurrencies is to offer a decentralized alternative to traditional financial infrastructure with middlemen. In this way, costs and risks, such as blockages and censorship, are reduced. And yet, here we are again, with digital assets reentering the traditional financial world in the form of Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs).

An ETF is an investment vehicle whose shares trade on a stock exchange. In other words, it’s an asset that represents something else without direct exposure —in this case, cryptocurrencies. Spot products hold the underlying crypto, while futures products use contracts linked to its price.

So far, coins like Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH), and Ripple (XRP) have their own ETF products available for investors. There’s a lot of money in there, too. According to CoinStats, crypto ETFs have over $171 billion of Assets Under Management (AUM).

Such a fact begs the question: is this really beneficial for the want-to-be decentralized crypto world, or is it just a blatant invasion from the old financial system? Let’s explore this topic.

The first thing we must consider is that crypto-related ETFs are not cryptocurrency themselves, in any way, shape, or form. Instead, with a spot ETF, the investor owns shares in a financial product that holds the underlying asset.

That means there’s a company (or another middleman) behind this product, handling all the real coins on your behalf —but you’ll never see the real coins themselves. Future-based products don’t even have third-party coins, and only obtain exposure through financial contracts.

Investing in a crypto ETF isn’t the same as “owning” crypto. You’re basically buying a ticket that represents a certain amount of gold, but it’s not, and it’ll never be, the gold itself. The value of that ticket is completely out of your control, and the middleman who sells these tickets takes a nice cut for handling them. If we think about it in simple terms, that’s it, that’s a crypto ETF.

Well, put that way, it sounds almost like a scam—though, of course, it isn't. There are many people, and especially institutions, that cannot or don’t wish to manage their own "gold" (their own cryptocurrencies). This investment vehicle is a service that offers them greater security and convenience, allowing them to gain some exposure without the major risks. After all, self-custody has its perils, too.

Self-custody requires work and responsibility, while many investors are more familiar with the brokerage environment. They often rely on regulated middlemen to handle sensitive financial transactions, and they’re comfortable within this system. Big companies, especially, aren’t suddenly learning how to properly set up and store a cold wallet with millions of dollars inside. Instead, they’re hiring the services or buying the products of experts in the matter, if they want to add crypto to their portfolios.

Therefore, trust is something ETFs can bring to the crypto world. And regulated trust is what institutions are usually looking for. Institutional participation can bring more liquidity (always a good thing) and connect crypto markets with traditional finance. The scale of recent inflows shows that these products have become an important bridge between the two worlds. As described by CoinStats, there was an inflow of over $5.2 billion to crypto ETFs in August alone.

Regulated investment products like ETFs introduce disclosure, reporting, and oversight requirements that many crypto platforms have historically lacked, so that’s why institutions may prefer them over self-custody. Access can be easier too, since you can buy through a traditional brokerage account. Someone else is responsible for every difficult part, and you just handle your investment. It’s fast and not cheap, but convenient.

Convenience is not synonymous with security—not by a long shot. Exchanges can be hacked or go bankrupt. The same can happen to other custodians, such as the firms behind ETFs. But beyond that lies the risk of the crypto industry’s sudden centralization. As we’ve mentioned above, crypto ETFs have over $171 billion AUM. That’s barely 6.5% of the whole cryptocurrency market cap… for now. We need to check the potential rise of these figures, too.

Since their inception in 2024, that same percentage has been growing. As we can see from CMC data, the AUM as a percentage of market cap started at 2.6% in 2024. Then, it was 5.8% in 2025, and now here we are. If they keep up like this, their average growth rate would be around 1.9% per year.

Does this mean ETFs and the firms behind them will take over most of the crypto industry in some years? It’s highly unlikely. At this rate, they’d need a stagnant crypto market capitalization and at least 23 years to reach 51%. However, it’s still concerning that billions in crypto arepooling towards centralized institutions, which could give them substantial power over decentralized crypto networks.

Especially in Proof-of-Stake (PoS) networks like Ethereum or Cardano, “validators” stake (lock) a certain amount to have the right to approve/reject transactions, partake in governance voting, and receive rewards. The more they stake, the more power they have. In a grim scenario, if an ETF brand decides to stake its billions, it could potentially manipulate entire networks. Smaller networks, with fewer community members and nodes, are the most vulnerable.

Centralization around the rules of a single country may also be possible, given that ETFs are products regulated according to their region. Currently, according to ETFLlama, the vast majority (144) are domiciled in Switzerland, followed by the US (76) and the EU (59). However, measured by Assets Under Management (AUM), the leaders are the US ($114.7 billion), Switzerland ($5.53 billion), and the UK ($5.36 billion).

A current reality is that ETFs have to comply with their country's laws, and that could mean censorship for certain users of PoS networks. For instance, for those listed by OFAC in the US. The fact is that the presence of big, powerful players always entails risks, and cryptocurrencies were created precisely to avoid those risks.

Crypto ETFs show how far digital assets have moved into traditional finance. They make access easier and attract institutional money, but every layer of intermediation can also concentrate control. That matters because decentralization is more than a technical feature.

It’s about keeping control distributed, reducing dependence on institutions, and preserving the ability to transact without asking a financial intermediary for permission. Obyte, for instance, takes this idea further by using a DAG-based network without miners or “validators”. There are no block producers deciding which transactions enter the ledger, creating a different model for distributing control across the network.

Now, ETFs can coexist with decentralized cryptocurrencies, and they can bring useful access to people who prefer traditional financial products. Yet the more crypto moves through centralized gateways, the more important its underlying decentralized infrastructure becomes. For projects like Obyte, maintaining that decentralization is part of the point itself. It keeps the original idea of crypto alive: giving users more direct control over their digital assets and transactions.

So, the ideal approach is to strike a balance. We can perfectly well coexist with the traditional financial system and benefit mutually, while remembering why cryptocurrencies exist in the first place and choosing those that are best for the job. After all, self-custody and direct, disintermediated control are the only things that grant us freedom and ownership.

#9603. This Chain Was Dunkin's Bitter Rival In The '50s — Now It's The Most Popular Donut Spot In Japan

Dunkin' is one of America's favorite spots to grab a quick donut and one of its famous syrup-infused iced coffees — which we ranked from worst to best. Today, the chain boasts more than 10,000 stores in the U.S. alone and sits comfortably at the top of the country's donut hierarchy. However, it wasn't always the undisputed heavyweight. In a rivalry that gives McDonald's and Burger King a run for their money, Dunkin' spent decades going head-to-head with Mister Donut. Ultimately, Dunkin' came out on top — at least, if we're talking strictly about the USA. Over in Japan, Mister Donut reigns supreme.

What makes this feud particularly fascinating is that it was a family affair. Dunkin', originally known as Dunkin' Donuts, was founded in 1950 by William Rosenberg. The simple combination of donuts and coffee proved to be a huge success. Naturally, Rosenberg wanted to expand the business through franchising. So far, so good, right? Well, not everyone was happy with the idea, including Harry Winokur, Rosenberg's brother-in-law. In a move that would spark a decades-long rivalry, Winokur left the business and opened Mister Donut just a few miles from Dunkin's original location. He even embraced franchising, with Mister Donut employees reportedly being prohibited from saying the word "dunk" in their stores.

As is often the case, feuds rarely end with a clear winner. In 1990, Dunkin' acquired Mister Donut and rebranded nearly all of its American locations as Dunkin' stores (ouch). Today, just one Mister Donut location remains in the U.S. That must have been a hit on Winokur's pride, but while Dunkin' was busy making cereal in the '80s, Mister Donut was thriving on the other side of the world. Today, Mister Donut is Japan's leading donut chain, with more than 900 locations in operation.

Japan has embraced plenty of Western-style foods with open arms. Think of the juicy, hamburger-inspired hambāgu, or comforting pizza toast with its wide array of toppings. Mister Donut also happens to fit comfortably into this category. However, one thing worth knowing about Japan's take on Western staples is that they're rarely direct copies. Instead, the country has a knack for putting its own spin on imported dishes. That's exactly how Mister Donut managed to carve out a place for itself in the market.

The first Mister Donut opened its doors in Japan in 1971, after business executive Seiichi Suzuki acquired the exclusive rights to operate the brand in the country. The original menu featured familiar American favorites, but Suzuki also introduced items and adjustments designed to appeal to local tastes. These included reducing the sugar content of certain products, serving more modest portions, and creating a cozy, sit-down atmosphere. The approach proved successful, and Mister Donut quickly expanded across Japan. Dunkin', meanwhile, had also tried its luck in the Japanese market, opening its first location in 1970. While Mister Donut continued to grow, Dunkin' struggled to gain a foothold and eventually left Japan altogether in 1998.

In 1989, Suzuki's company Duskin acquired full ownership of Mister Donut's Japanese operations, giving it greater freedom to develop the brand's distinctly Japanese identity. From there, the chain continued to expand, eventually bringing its donuts to markets including Thailand, Australia, Taiwan, and Singapore. Today, Mister Donut is best known for its playful, distinctly Japanese creations, particularly the Pon De Ring, a chewy, ring-shaped donut made up of small dough balls, and Mocchurin, its mochi-inspired donut line that is so soft, they require paper trays to keep each donut from losing its shape.

#9602. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!
